clinicalPearls: Caused by Pythium insidiosum, an aquatic oomycete (water mould) rather than a true fungus, so it lacks ergosterol and responds poorly to conventional antifungal drugs
Acquired from warm freshwater and wetland environments, typically in tropical and subtropical regions, through skin or corneal contact with the motile zoospores
Vascular pythiosis is the most feared form: an aggressive angioinvasive arteritis, often of the lower limbs, seen especially in patients with thalassaemia or other haemoglobinopathies
Keratitis is another major form, presenting as a progressive, treatment-resistant corneal ulcer in contact-lens wearers or after ocular trauma involving water exposure
Cutaneous and subcutaneous granulomatous lesions and gastrointestinal disease are also described
Diagnosis is difficult because the broad, sparsely septate hyphae mimic zygomycetes on histology; culture, serology, and molecular methods aid identification
Management combines aggressive surgery, often radical excision or amputation for vascular disease, with antifungal-type agents and immunotherapy, as drugs alone rarely cure it
reference.pathophysiology: Pythium insidiosum is an oomycete that thrives in stagnant fresh water and colonises aquatic plants. It releases biflagellate motile zoospores that are attracted to and encyst on damaged skin, cornea, or the gut wall, then germinate to produce invasive hyphae. Because its cell wall is built of cellulose and beta-glucans and its membranes lack ergosterol, the organism is intrinsically resistant to antifungal agents that target ergosterol synthesis. In the vascular form the hyphae invade arterial walls, provoking a necrotising, thrombosing arteritis that progressively occludes vessels and produces limb ischaemia; the tendency for this angioinvasive disease is greatly increased in patients with thalassaemia and iron overload. Host immune responses are largely granulomatous and eosinophil-rich but insufficient to contain the aggressive tissue invasion.
additionalDifferentials: Mucormycosis and other angioinvasive mould infections
Fungal keratitis from Fusarium or Aspergillus species
Peripheral arterial occlusive disease or vasculitis
Eosinophilic gastrointestinal disease in the intestinal form
additionalInvestigations: Histopathology with special stains showing broad, sparsely septate, right-angle-branching hyphae resembling zygomycetes
Culture of tissue on suitable media with demonstration of zoospore formation in water
Serological assays (immunodiffusion, ELISA) for anti-Pythium antibodies
Molecular identification by PCR and sequencing of the ribosomal region
Arterial imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT or MR angiography) to define vascular involvement
Corneal scrapings and confocal microscopy in suspected keratitis
redFlags: Rapidly progressive limb ischaemia or arterial occlusion from angioinvasive disease
A corneal ulcer worsening despite standard antifungal or antibacterial therapy
Underlying thalassaemia or haemoglobinopathy with freshwater exposure
Evidence of proximal vascular or disseminated spread
reference.prognosis: Vascular pythiosis carries a high risk of limb loss and death unless there is early radical surgery combined with medical and immunotherapy; ocular disease often leads to loss of the eye, whereas localised cutaneous disease treated promptly has a better outcome.
pitfalls: Treating as mucormycosis or ordinary fungal disease with antifungals alone, since the oomycete resists ergosterol-targeting drugs
Delaying surgery in vascular disease in the hope that medical therapy will suffice
Failing to recognise thalassaemia as a strong risk factor prompting earlier suspicion
Misidentifying the hyphae histologically and missing the diagnosis
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
